summary: Describes NETCRT, a character display protocol, now revised after circulation at the May meeting. It was created because Rand wanted network access to URSA, UCLA CCN's display-based conversational remote job entry system, used to enter and edit programs and examine output.

eli5.summary: A way to use a faraway computer from a screen of letters: type your work, send it, and read the results, all through a network.

questions: how does a virtual character display work
subtitle: Virtual display terminal protocol for remote interactive systems

tldr.problem: UCLA's URSA system required interactive display terminal control, but simple text protocols like Telnet were not adequate for its text editor and real-time feedback.
tldr.mechanism: NETCRT defines a virtual character display (VCD) with a screen, local buffer, cursor register, and control commands. The server sends commands to write, read, erase and position the cursor; the client responds with screen content and keyboard events.
tldr.outcome: NETCRT remained a site-specific protocol for UCLA's URSA system. The concepts influenced later full-screen terminal protocols but were not adopted network-wide.

today: NETCRT was implemented at UCLA for URSA but did not become a widespread standard. Later character-oriented terminal protocols such as ANSI escape sequences evolved differently. However, NETCRT's ideas about screen control and state synchronization influenced the design space for remote display protocols.

sections.title: Purpose and Design
sections.content:
RFC 205 describes NETCRT, a protocol for UCLA Campus Computing Network (CCN) to provide network access to URSA, its display-based remote job entry system. URSA's text editor requires fast, fine-grained control over a character display and cannot work with a simple typewriter-like Telnet connection.

NETCRT introduces the concept of a virtual character display (VCD), which simulates a CCI 301 or IBM 2260 display terminal. The VCD has a rectangular buffer of characters, a cursor register, a keyboard, and a state machine. This abstraction allows a remote user's terminal to appear local to URSA.
sections.eli5: NETCRT pretends the faraway computer has a real screen sitting on the desk. The server can write words, move a cursor, and read what the user types.

sections.title: Virtual Character Display Model
sections.content:
The VCD has two states: Local (keyboard unlocked, user control) and Control (keyboard locked, server control). The user enters Control state by pressing Transmit, Break, or responding to a server break request. The VCD returns to Local state when the user presses Reset or the server sends a LOCAL command.

The display buffer is a two-dimensional array of M columns and N rows, addressed linearly from 0 to M×N−1. The cursor register points to the current position. Text overwrites the buffer at the cursor and advances it; a newline moves to the start of the next line. The server can save and restore the cursor position in a register.
sections.eli5: The display is like a grid of letters. A cursor (a blinking spot) marks where new letters go. The server can save where the cursor is, move it, write text, read back what is there.

sections.title: Commands and Message Flow
sections.content:
The server issues command segments to the VCD: ERASE (clear buffer), BLANK (disable refresh), CURSOR (position cursor), WRITE (put text at cursor), READ (fetch text from buffer), SAVE (store cursor), RESTORE (restore cursor). The VCD responds with data when READ commands request it.

Break synchronization is critical. When the server issues a break (INS), it also sends a SYNC command on the data link. The VCD buffers commands but on receiving INS or SYNC, it enters Control state and ignores LOCAL commands until SYNC arrives, ensuring the server regains control even if commands were queued. This handles the race between network delays and server needs.
sections.eli5: The server tells the display what to do: erase it, write here, read that area, move the cursor. Breaks let the server interrupt if the user pressed a key.
